title: SCID Management: Live-Vaccine Rules, Household Contacts and Stem-Cell Gene Therapy
summary: Learn why a child with suspected severe combined immunodeficiency gets no live vaccines while the household is vaccinated as usual, what autologous CD34+ gene therapy for ADA-SCID and SCID-X1 actually involves, and how big the IUIS catalogue of inborn errors of immunity has become.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 52 Hits 14 and 15 and Trap 1, checked against the CDC/ACIP Altered Immunocompetence best-practice page, Aiuti 2017, Blanco 2020, Cesana 2024, van der Burg 2019 and the IUIS classification updates (Tangye 2020, Tangye 2022, Poli 2025). Discrepancies recorded: the reviewer’s “IUIS 2020: 430 disorders in 10 categories; 65 newly added” is the 2019 update (430 genetic defects causing 404 diseases, 64 new gene defects) and is superseded by 508 genes plus 17 phenocopies in the 2024 update (register rv-iuis-2024-count); the reviewer’s one-line gene-therapy description omits non-myeloablative busulfan conditioning and the vector-driven T-cell leukaemias (register rv-scid-gt-insertional-leukemia); the household-contact guidance is US CDC/ACIP and Philippine rules are not covered (register rv-scid-household-live-vaccines). Not taught and left pending: the reviewer’s claim that JAK3 and γc SCID are distinguished rapidly by protein assays and that gene therapy is effective only in γc SCID. Ch. 52 TREC screening, lymphocyte thresholds and the other named immunodeficiencies are taught in the other Ch. 52 lessons.

objectives: Apply the live-vaccine rule to a child with suspected severe immunodeficiency and, separately, to the household contacts.
Describe what autologous CD34+ stem-cell gene therapy for ADA-SCID and SCID-X1 involves, including conditioning and the insertional-mutagenesis risk.
State how the IUIS catalogue of inborn errors of immunity is organised and how its count has changed.

scenes.title: The screen is positive — now what?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a 3-week-old boy was flagged by an abnormal newborn TREC screen and confirmatory flow cytometry shows almost no T cells. Three questions arrive the same morning: (1) the rotavirus dose is due at 2 months — give it? (2) his 4-year-old sister is due for MMR and varicella — hold them? (3) the parents have read about a gene-therapy cure and ask whether it is “just an infusion”. Question token: “Who gets vaccinated, and what does gene therapy really involve?”

cues.text: A three-week-old boy was flagged by the newborn screen for severe combined immunodeficiency, and confirmatory testing shows almost no T cells.
Three questions arrive the same morning: his rotavirus dose, his sister’s measles and varicella vaccines, and the gene-therapy cure the parents have read about.
Who gets vaccinated here, and what does gene therapy actually involve?

scenes.title: One gene, one catalogue, one hazard
scenes.altText: Schematic: a card showing that inborn errors of immunity are defined as disease caused by damaging germline variants in single genes, catalogued by the IUIS expert committee in ten tables; the 2019 update (published 2020) listed 430 genetic defects causing 404 diseases, with 64 new gene defects in two years; the 2022 update reached 485; the 2024 update lists 508 genes plus 17 phenocopies. A second card: untreated SCID infants are born asymptomatic, develop severe opportunistic infection and failure to thrive within the first month, and are vulnerable to secondary infection caused by live vaccines.

cues.text: Inborn errors of immunity are defined as disease caused by damaging variants in single genes, and an expert committee of the International Union of Immunological Societies keeps the catalogue in ten tables.

The 2019 update, published in 2020, listed four hundred and thirty genetic defects causing four hundred and four diseases, with sixty-four new gene defects in two years. The catalogue keeps growing: four hundred and eighty-five in 2022, and five hundred and eight genes plus seventeen phenocopies in the 2024 update.
Severe combined immunodeficiency sits in the first of those tables. Babies are born looking well, then within the first month develop severe opportunistic infection and failure to thrive.
And they are vulnerable to a second kind of infection: the one a live vaccine gives them. That single sentence drives the whole management plan.

scenes.title: Shield the baby, arm the household
scenes.altText: Two-column rule card. The patient: persons with most forms of altered immunocompetence should not receive live vaccines — MMR, varicella, MMRV, live attenuated influenza, yellow fever, oral Ty21a typhoid, BCG, smallpox and rotavirus; severe cell-mediated immunodeficiency means no live viral or live bacterial vaccine at all, and for rotavirus the T-lymphocyte data specifically concern SCID. Non-live vaccines are safe in altered immunocompetence, although they may be less effective. The household: contacts should receive all age- and exposure-appropriate vaccines except smallpox vaccine; live MMR, varicella and rotavirus should be given to susceptible contacts when indicated; the only specific precaution is a rash after varicella vaccine, when direct contact is avoided until the rash resolves; everyone washes hands after changing the nappy of a rotavirus-vaccinated infant because shedding can last up to a month. Timing card: in a North American consortium series, infants transplanted before 3.5 months had 94% survival, against 50% for those transplanted later with active infection.

cues.text: Rule one, the patient. People with most forms of altered immunocompetence should not receive live vaccines: measles-mumps-rubella, varicella, live attenuated influenza, yellow fever, oral typhoid, BCG, smallpox and rotavirus. For severe cell-mediated immunodeficiency the rule is absolute, and the rotavirus data behind it come specifically from severe combined immunodeficiency.
Non-live vaccines are not a safety problem here. They can be given, but they may simply not work while the immune system is failing.

Rule two, the household. Contacts should receive every age-appropriate vaccine except smallpox vaccine, and that includes the live measles, varicella and rotavirus vaccines. Vaccinating the family is protection, not a threat: a family member who never catches measles cannot carry it home.

Only two practical precautions: if a varicella vaccine recipient develops a rash, avoid direct contact until it resolves, and everyone washes their hands after nappy changes, because rotavirus vaccine shedding can last up to a month. Meanwhile the clock matters — in one consortium series, infants transplanted before three and a half months had ninety-four percent survival, against fifty percent for those transplanted later with an active infection.

scenes.title: What gene therapy actually is
scenes.altText: Schematic of the gene-therapy pathway and its two case histories. ADA-SCID: autologous bone-marrow CD34+ cells transduced with a gamma-retroviral vector carrying ADA, given after non-myeloablative busulfan to make marrow space; marketing approval in the European Union in 2016 was based on 18 children treated between 2000 and 2011 with a median follow-up of about 7 years, survival 100%, gene marking averaging 70% in T cells but only 1–2% in CD34+ cells, and no concurrent enzyme replacement therapy. Earlier attempts without conditioning gave low marking and patients stayed on enzyme replacement. SCID-X1: first-generation gamma-retroviral vectors without conditioning restored T cells but left B and NK recovery weak, and six children developed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia 2–14 years later through vector-driven insertional mutagenesis; lentiviral vectors with low-dose busulfan now give sustained T, B and NK recovery. In 2024 one ADA-SCID recipient also developed T-ALL, 4.7 years after gene therapy, from a single vector insertion activating LMO2.

cues.text: Gene therapy here is not a simple infusion. The patient’s own CD34-positive stem cells are collected, a working copy of the gene is inserted with a viral vector, and the cells are returned after low-dose busulfan has made space in the marrow.

For adenosine deaminase deficiency that package won European marketing approval in 2016, on eighteen children treated between 2000 and 2011 with about seven years of median follow-up: survival one hundred percent, no concurrent enzyme replacement, gene marking around seventy percent in T cells but only one to two percent in stem cells. Earlier attempts without conditioning marked too few cells, and those patients stayed on enzyme replacement.

For X-linked disease, the first vectors without conditioning restored T cells but left B and natural killer recovery weak — and six children developed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia two to fourteen years later, because the vector switched on a neighbouring oncogene.

Lentiviral vectors with low-dose busulfan now restore T, B and natural killer cells. But in 2024 one adenosine deaminase patient also developed T-cell leukaemia, four point seven years after treatment, so follow-up never stops.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A child with suspected severe immunodeficiency is due for vaccines — give them on schedule” (✓ no live vaccines until severe immunodeficiency is excluded; non-live ones may be given but may not work); “Hold the family’s vaccines too, to protect the baby” (✓ the opposite — household contacts get every age-appropriate vaccine except smallpox, including live MMR, varicella and rotavirus); “Gene therapy is an infusion of corrected cells with no conditioning and no cancer risk” (✓ non-myeloablative busulfan is part of the protocol, and vector-driven insertional mutagenesis has caused T-cell leukaemia).

cues.text: Trap one: the baby is due for vaccines, so give them on schedule. No. No live vaccine until severe immunodeficiency has been excluded.
Trap two: hold the family’s vaccines as well. The opposite is true — household contacts should receive every age-appropriate vaccine except smallpox, including the live ones.
Trap three: gene therapy is just an infusion with no risk. No. Conditioning is part of the protocol, and vector insertion has caused leukaemia.

props.title: ✗ “Vaccinate the baby on schedule.”
lines: ✓ No live vaccines until SCID is excluded

scenes.title: Shield the baby, arm the house
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “SHIELD the baby — no live vaccines; ARM the house — every age-appropriate vaccine except smallpox; READ THE SMALL PRINT on gene therapy — busulfan first, and watch the insertion site for years.” Three tokens: shield, arm, small print. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: shield the baby — no live vaccines. Arm the house — every age-appropriate vaccine except smallpox. And read the small print on gene therapy: busulfan first, then watch the insertion site for years.

Where it breaks: “arm the house” is United States guidance and has its own precautions, a rash after varicella vaccine and hand washing after nappy changes; “shield” does not mean withholding non-live vaccines, which are safe though often ineffective; and gene therapy is available only for particular genotypes at particular centres.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Patient: no live vaccines · household: all age-appropriate except smallpox”, “Gene therapy = autologous CD34+ cells + vector + busulfan, with long-term leukaemia watch”.

cues.text: A newborn flagged by the severe combined immunodeficiency screen must receive no live vaccines while the household is kept fully vaccinated, and the autologous stem cell gene therapies that can cure adenosine deaminase deficient and X-linked disease need marrow conditioning and long-term watching for vector-driven leukaemia.

props.label: Patient: no live vaccines · household: all except smallpox
Gene therapy = CD34+ cells + vector + busulfan + long watch

explanation.what: Plain language: a baby whose immune system cannot fight anything must not be given a vaccine made of living, weakened germs — but the people around the baby should be vaccinated, because a vaccinated family cannot bring the real disease home. Gene therapy fixes the baby’s own marrow cells outside the body and gives them back, after drugs make room for them. Scientific terms: inborn errors of immunity (IEI), severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), altered immunocompetence, live attenuated viral and bacterial vaccines, autologous CD34+ haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, gamma-retroviral and lentiviral vectors, non-myeloablative busulfan conditioning, insertional mutagenesis, T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL).
explanation.why: Live vaccine organisms replicate unchecked in a child with severe cell-mediated immunodeficiency, so the vaccine itself becomes the infection; non-live vaccines carry no such safety risk but may not generate a response. Vaccinating contacts removes the household as a source of wild-type infection. Gene therapy works because corrected lymphoid cells have a survival advantage, but a vector that integrates next to a proto-oncogene can drive leukaemia years later.
explanation.measure: Patient: withhold MMR, varicella, MMRV, live attenuated influenza, yellow fever, oral Ty21a typhoid, BCG, smallpox and rotavirus; for rotavirus the T-lymphocyte contraindication data concern SCID. Household: all age- and exposure-appropriate vaccines except smallpox vaccine, including live MMR, varicella and rotavirus; avoid direct contact if a varicella vaccinee develops a rash, and wash hands after nappy changes because rotavirus shedding may last up to a month. Gene therapy for ADA-SCID: autologous bone-marrow CD34+ cells, gamma-retroviral vector, non-myeloablative busulfan; EU approval 2016 on 18 children treated 2000–2011, median follow-up about 7 years, 100% survival, T-cell gene marking averaging 70% at 1 year against 1–2% in CD34+ cells. SCID-X1: six T-ALL cases 2–14 years after the first unconditioned gamma-retroviral trials; lentiviral vectors with low-dose busulfan now restore T, B and NK cells.
explanation.differs: Patient vs household vaccination; live vs non-live vaccines (safety vs effectiveness); ADA-SCID gene therapy (approved product, conditioning, enzyme replacement stopped) vs SCID-X1 gene therapy (first trials unconditioned, leukaemia, now lentiviral); 430 genetic defects in the 2019 IUIS update vs 508 genes in the 2024 update.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the vaccine question about a screen-positive infant and the family, identifying which vaccines are live, or recognising insertional mutagenesis as the late complication of retroviral gene therapy.

mnemonic.text: SHIELD the baby — no live vaccines. ARM the house — every age-appropriate vaccine except smallpox. READ THE SMALL PRINT on gene therapy — busulfan first, then watch the insertion site for years.
mnemonic.explanation: Keeps the patient rule and the contact rule from collapsing into one another, and keeps gene therapy from sounding like a simple infusion.
mnemonic.limitation: “Arm the house” is United States CDC/ACIP guidance and carries its own precautions (rash after varicella vaccine, hand washing after nappy changes); “shield” does not mean withholding non-live vaccines, which are safe though often ineffective; and gene therapy is available only for particular genotypes at particular centres.

takeaway: A newborn flagged by the severe combined immunodeficiency screen must receive no live vaccines while the household is kept fully vaccinated, and the autologous stem cell gene therapies that can cure adenosine deaminase deficient and X-linked disease need marrow conditioning and long-term watching for vector-driven leukaemia.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant has an abnormal newborn screen and confirmatory testing consistent with severe combined immunodeficiency. His 4-year-old sister is due for MMR and varicella vaccines. What is the correct advice?

options.text: Withhold live vaccines from the infant; give the sister her age-appropriate vaccines, including MMR and varicella
options.rationale: Correct. Household contacts should receive all age- and exposure-appropriate vaccines except smallpox vaccine, and live MMR, varicella and rotavirus should be given to susceptible contacts when indicated.

options.text: Withhold all vaccines from everyone in the household until the infant is treated
options.rationale: Incorrect. Leaving contacts unvaccinated exposes the infant to wild-type disease; only smallpox vaccine is excluded for contacts.

options.text: Give the infant his live vaccines early so immunity develops before transplant
options.rationale: Incorrect. Persons with severe cell-mediated immunodeficiency should not receive live viral or live bacterial vaccines, which can replicate unchecked.

options.text: Give the sister only inactivated vaccines and defer MMR and varicella indefinitely
options.rationale: Incorrect. The live MMR and varicella vaccines should be given to susceptible household contacts; the only precaution is avoiding direct contact if the varicella vaccinee develops a rash.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes autologous gene therapy as used for ADA-SCID and SCID-X1?

options.text: The patient’s own CD34+ cells are transduced with a vector carrying the normal gene and returned after non-myeloablative conditioning
options.rationale: Correct. Conditioning (low-dose busulfan) to make marrow space was the breakthrough that allowed durable engraftment of gene-corrected progenitors.

options.text: A vector carrying the normal gene is injected intravenously to transduce the thymus directly
options.rationale: Incorrect. The described protocols are ex vivo: cells are collected, transduced outside the body and reinfused.

options.text: Donor CD34+ cells from a matched sibling are transduced before transplantation
options.rationale: Incorrect. The cells are autologous, which is precisely why no donor is needed.

options.text: Mature donor T cells are gene-corrected and infused repeatedly for life
options.rationale: Incorrect. Early work did infuse transduced autologous lymphocytes, but current stem-cell gene therapy is a single infusion of the patient’s own corrected CD34+ cells.

questions.stem: Several children treated in the first SCID-X1 gamma-retroviral gene-therapy trials developed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia 2 to 14 years afterwards. What is the accepted mechanism?

options.text: Vector integration near a proto-oncogene activating it (insertional mutagenesis)
options.rationale: Correct. Enhancer sequences in the vector long terminal repeats can switch on neighbouring genes such as LMO2.
Incorrect. The leukaemias were traced to integration sites, not to a replicating vector.
Incorrect. The first SCID-X1 trials used no conditioning at all, and leukaemia still occurred.

options.text: Graft-versus-host disease from the infused cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. The cells are the patient’s own, so graft-versus-host disease is not the mechanism.

claims.text: Live viral and bacterial vaccines are withheld in severe cell-mediated immunodeficiency; the listed live vaccines; non-live vaccines are safe but may be ineffective; rotavirus contraindication data concern SCID.
Household contacts receive all age- and exposure-appropriate vaccines except smallpox, including live MMR, varicella and rotavirus; rash and nappy-change precautions.
Transplantation before 3.5 months of age gave 94% survival against 50% for later transplantation with active infection.
Inborn errors of immunity are single-gene disorders catalogued by IUIS in 10 tables; 430 genetic defects (404 diseases) in the 2019 update, 485 in 2022, 508 genes plus 17 phenocopies in 2024.

ADA-SCID gene therapy: autologous CD34+ cells, gamma-retroviral vector, non-myeloablative busulfan, EU approval 2016, 18 children, 100% survival, marking 70% T cells vs 1–2% CD34+, enzyme replacement not continued.
SCID-X1 gene therapy: unconditioned gamma-retroviral trials restored T cells with weak B and NK recovery; lentiviral vectors with low-dose busulfan restore T, B and NK.
Insertional mutagenesis caused T-ALL in six SCID-X1 recipients 2–14 years after gene therapy and in one ADA-SCID recipient 4.7 years after gene therapy (LMO2 activation).
Reviewer claim that JAK3 and γc SCID can be distinguished rapidly by protein assays and that gene therapy is effective only in γc/X-linked SCID.
claims.note: No open source read in this session supports the protein-assay triage or the γc-only restriction, so it is not taught.

claims.text: Scenario invented; pathway and rule cards are schematic.
“Shield the baby, arm the house, read the small print.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 15 gives “IUIS 2020: 430 disorders in 10 categories” with 65 newly added. Tangye 2020 (the 2019 update) reports 430 known genetic defects causing 404 diseases, with 64 new gene defects; the count has since risen to 485 (2022) and 508 genes plus 17 phenocopies (2024 update, Poli 2025). The lesson teaches the count with its edition.

Hit 14 describes gene therapy as “autologous CD34+ stem cells + retroviral vector” restoring thymopoiesis, omitting the non-myeloablative busulfan conditioning that made durable engraftment possible (Aiuti 2017) and the vector-driven T-cell leukaemias — six SCID-X1 recipients 2–14 years after treatment (Blanco 2020) and one ADA-SCID recipient 4.7 years after treatment (Cesana 2024) — as well as the shift to lentiviral vectors.

Trap 1’s household-contact rule is United States CDC/ACIP guidance; Philippine immunisation rules are not covered and MTLE candidates should check local requirements. The CDC page states smallpox vaccine as the exception for contacts and adds precautions the reviewer omits (avoid direct contact if a varicella vaccinee develops a rash; hand washing after nappy changes because rotavirus shedding may last up to a month).
